findings: Bilateral lungs are well-expanded and predominantly clear with no focal consolidation, mass, or pleural effusion identified

Bilateral costal cartilage calcification is present, appearing dense and irregular/lobulated along the rib margins bilaterally, most prominent at the lower ribs and costodiaphragmatic regions — pattern consistent with enchondral ('eggshell' or lobular) calcification
The cardiac silhouette appears normal in size, with a cardiothoracic ratio estimated less than 0.5
The mediastinum is midline and of normal width; trachea is central
Both hemidiaphragms are visualized; right hemidiaphragm is slightly higher than left, which is normal
Bony thorax: multiple ribs demonstrate extensive bilateral costal cartilage calcifications; no acute rib fracture identified
Aortic knuckle is visible but not enlarged
differential: Extensive bilateral costal cartilage calcification — most likely age-related (dystrophic) calcification, a normal variant in older individuals
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) — can cause cartilage calcification with similar radiographic appearance
Ochronosis (alkaptonuria) — rare cause of extensive cartilage calcification, though typically also affects intervertebral discs and other cartilage
anatomyConcerns: The costal cartilage calcifications are bilateral and extensive, which is an unusual degree and distribution that warrants clinical correlation to exclude a metabolic or systemic cause, though age-related calcification remains most likely
No significant acquisition inconsistencies noted; the image is adequately exposed and positioned for a PA chest radiograph
